title: The Lord's Day
hook: every Sunday is a little Easter

segments.voice: Yesterday, Saturday for Mary and its votive Mass, the day of waiting before the morning. Your line was saturday is hers. Did you give it a quiet minute? Day six hundred ninety-three.

It's very early. A few women are walking out of Jerusalem carrying spices, worried about one practical thing: who will roll the stone away from the tomb? The Sabbath is over. It's the first day of the week, and the sun is coming up. When they get there, Mark says, the stone is already rolled back, and the tomb is empty. Out of that one morning, Christians built a habit that comes round every week. Today, the day itself.
screen: `VERY EARLY, CARRYING SPICES.` → `THE FIRST DAY OF THE WEEK.` → `A WEEKLY HABIT.`

segments.voice: Each of the four Gospels puts the empty tomb early on the first day of the week. So the first day became the Christians' day. In Acts, the disciples at Troas, with Paul visiting, gather on the first day of the week to break bread. And the last book of the Bible gives the day its name. John, on the island of Patmos, writes in the Douay-Rheims: "I was in the spirit on the Lord's day." In the Latin of the Church, Sunday is still Dominica, the Lord's. Justin Martyr, writing to the Roman emperor, described what Christians did on the day called Sunday: they gathered from town and country, heard the writings of the apostles and prophets, prayed, and shared bread and wine, and a collection went to widows and orphans. Catholics reading it today recognize the Mass. Catholics speak of every Sunday as a little Easter: not a reminder of Easter, they say, but the same feast, coming round every seven days. The Second Vatican Council called Sunday the original feast day, the foundation of the whole year. Some early writers gave it another name: the eighth day. The old week ended with the Sabbath, the seventh day; they saw the resurrection as the first day of a new creation, a day outside the old count. Catholics keep it in two ways. They go to Mass, which the Church asks of them as an obligation. And they rest, setting aside work that gets in the way of worship, joy and family. Pope John Paul the Second wrote a whole letter on it in 1998, Dies Domini, the day of the Lord. And this ends week ninety-nine: the Lateran, Christ the King, the months with their themes, then Friday, the Ember days, Mary's Saturday, and now Sunday, the day the whole week leans toward.
screen: `THE FIRST DAY OF THE WEEK.` · `I WAS IN THE SPIRIT ON THE LORD'S DAY.` · `JUSTIN DESCRIBES SUNDAY.` · `THE EIGHTH DAY: A NEW CREATION.` · then, large: `A LITTLE EASTER, EVERY SEVEN DAYS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan one piece of real rest for this Sunday. Settle, and breathe. Picture next Sunday from morning to night. Where's the noise, the errands, the inbox? Choose one thing to set down for that day: a chore that can wait, a screen, a worry you'll pick up on Monday. Then choose one thing to put in its place: a long meal, a walk, a call to someone you love, Mass if you go. Hold that picture for the rest of the sit. The bell holds the time.
Dominica. Latin for the Lord's, the Church's own name for Sunday since John called it the Lord's day in Revelation. Today's word.
Your line: a little easter. This Sunday, when you wake, say it once before you check your phone, and keep the one thing you planned. Day six hundred ninety-three.

howItsDone: Catholics are asked to attend Mass every Sunday (or on Saturday evening) and to keep the day free of work that hinders worship, rest and time with family; many families also keep a shared Sunday meal.
